title: Nehruvian and Gandhian Perspectives

cards.h: Two visions of how India should develop
cards.b:
At independence India was poor, mostly rural and dependent on imports of machinery. Leaders agreed on ending poverty but disagreed on how. Two broad answers competed.

Nehru's answer: planned, state-led industrialisation, with heavy industry and science, inside a democratic framework. Gandhi's answer: village self-reliance, small-scale production, limited wants and moral economy.

The Nehruvian model won in policy, but Gandhian ideas survived in the Directive Principles (Articles 40, 43, 47, 48), in khadi and village industries, and in later debates on sustainability.

UPSC asks you to compare the two, to judge the planning era, and to explain why planning gave way to the market after 1991.

• Hind Swaraj (1909): modern industrial civilisation multiplies wants and destroys moral life. Machinery should serve people, not replace them.
  • Swadeshi and khadi: local production and self-reliance; the charkha as a symbol of dignity and employment.
  • Trusteeship: the rich should hold wealth as trustees for society, a non-violent alternative to both capitalism and class war.
  • Sarvodaya (welfare of all), from his reading of Ruskin's Unto This Last.
  • Village republics and decentralisation.

J.C. Kumarappa, Economy of Permanence (1945)

Gandhi's economist argued for an economy that lives within nature's limits. Shriman Narayan Agarwal's Gandhian Plan (1944) put these ideas into a plan: cottage industry, agriculture first and village self-sufficiency.

Later echoes: E.F. Schumacher's Small is Beautiful (1973) and today's environmental critiques of growth.

• Influenced by Fabian socialism and Soviet planning, but committed to parliamentary democracy and civil liberties.
  • Mixed economy: a public sector in the "commanding heights" (steel, power, heavy machinery) alongside private enterprise.
  • Socialistic pattern of society: adopted at the Avadi session of the Congress (1955).
  • Science and technology: IITs, atomic energy, and dams which Nehru called the "temples of modern India" (Bhakra Nangal, 1954).
  • Self-reliance: import substitution and building domestic capacity.

Nehru disagreed openly with Gandhi in their 1945 letters: he thought village India could not escape poverty without industry and modern science, while Gandhi held to Hind Swaraj.

• Pre-1947 plans: the Bombay Plan (1944, industrialists), the Gandhian Plan (1944), the People's Plan (M.N. Roy, 1944) and the Sarvodaya Plan (J.P. Narayan, 1950).
  • Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution, with the PM as chair. It was extra-constitutional. The National Development Council (1952) brought in Chief Ministers.
  • Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956: reserved key sectors for the State.
  • First Plan (1951-56): agriculture. Second Plan (1956-61): the Mahalanobis model, with priority to heavy industry.
  • Twelve Five-Year Plans in all (1951-2017). The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

Achievements: an industrial base, public institutions (IITs, ISRO's forerunners), dams and power, a democratic framework and modest but steady growth after colonial stagnation.

Failures:

  • Growth of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 1980, which Raj Krishna called the "Hindu rate of growth".
  • Neglect of agriculture and primary education; mass poverty persisted.
  • A "licence-permit raj" (a phrase linked to C. Rajagopalachari, who founded the pro-market Swatantra Party in 1959).
  • Inefficient public enterprises and rent-seeking.

Key critics and analysts

Jagdish Bhagwati and Padma Desai, India: Planning for Industrialization (1970): controls choked efficiency. Sukhamoy Chakravarty, Development Planning: The Indian Experience (1987): a balanced insider view. Francine Frankel, India's Political Economy, 1947-1977 (1978): planners wanted radical aims but avoided conflict with landed elites.

Pranab Bardhan, The Political Economy of Development in India (1984)

Three dominant proprietary classes (industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats) competed for subsidies. The State became a broker of their claims, leaving little for investment.

Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987)

India had a "weak-strong state". They distinguished command polity (state-led, as in the Nehru and Indira years) from demand polity (where voters and groups press the State). They also spoke of "bullock capitalists": middle farmers who became a political force.

Atul Kohli, State-Directed Development (2004)

Compared India with Korea and Brazil; India's state was "fragmented-multiclass", not focused enough to drive fast growth.

For the Gandhian view: it protected employment and the environment; it fits ideas of sustainable development and decentralisation; it valued dignity and limited wants. Kumarappa's "economy of permanence" anticipated ecological economics.

Against: with a large and growing population, village industry alone could not create enough jobs or defence capacity. Ambedkar rejected village romanticism, and Nehru thought it would lock India in poverty.

Middle ground: Gandhian influence lasted in the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), small-scale reservation (until it was phased out in the 2000s), the panchayats (73rd Amendment), MGNREGA's local works, and today's support for MSMEs and the "vocal for local" call.

• NITI Aayog (2015): a think tank, not an allocator of funds. Its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers; it prepares indices (SDG India Index, Export Preparedness) and the "Viksit Bharat 2047" vision.
  • The end of Five-Year Plans in 2017; the Finance Commission and ministries now handle transfers.
  • Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and production-linked incentives revive the language of self-reliance, but through private industry rather than the public sector.
  • Gandhian echoes: natural farming, millets, khadi sales and climate-sensitive growth.
  • Debate: some states and economists argue for a body like the old NDC to make planning more federal.

Structure: context of 1947; Gandhi (Hind Swaraj, trusteeship, Kumarappa); Nehru (mixed economy, Mahalanobis, Avadi); planning machinery; achievements and failures; political-economy explanations (Bardhan, Rudolphs, Frankel); legacy today (NITI Aayog, Atmanirbhar).
